paper.title: Metabolomic machine learning predictor for diagnosis and prognosis of gastric cancer

claims.text: Targeted plasma metabolomics of 702 samples (389 GC, 313 NGC) reveals a reprogrammed GC metabolic landscape; 45 metabolites differ between GC and NGC (Wilcoxon, FDR<0.05, FC>1.25 or <0.8) and fall into 3 trajectory clusters.
claims.location: Abstract; Results 'Reprogrammed plasma metabolic landscape in GC patients', p.3; Fig. 2

claims.text: A LASSO+random-forest 10-metabolite diagnostic model (10-DM) reaches AUROC 0.967 (95% CI 0.944-0.987), sensitivity 0.854, specificity 0.926 in test set 1.
claims.location: Results p.3; Fig. 3b; Methods 'Diagnostic prediction model'

claims.text: The 10-DM model validates in an external test set (Cohort 2) with AUROC 0.920, sensitivity 0.905, specificity 0.75.

The 10-DM model detects early-stage GC: stage IA accuracy 90.9% (AUROC 0.957, sens 0.813, spec 0.926) and stage IB accuracy 0.927 (AUROC 0.984, sens 1, spec 0.926) in test set 1; stage IA accuracy 79.1% (AUROC 0.909) in test set 2.
The 10-DM model outperforms the routine 3-biomarker panel (CA19-9, CA72-4, CEA): sensitivity 0.925 vs 0.428 (any-one-abnormal rule), and single-marker sensitivities 0.217/0.317/0.165.
claims.location: Results 'Comparison of the diagnostic performance...', p.3; Supplementary Fig. 4a,b

claims.text: The 10-DM model outperforms SVM, logistic regression, random forest and PLS-DA models built in MetaboAnalyst on the same data.
claims.location: Results p.3; Supplementary Fig. 4c; Methods 'Diagnostic prediction model'

claims.text: A 28-metabolite random-survival-forest prognostic model (28-PM) predicts GC outcome in the test set with AUROC 0.832 (95% CI 0.697-0.951), sensitivity 0.900, specificity 0.700 and c-index 0.83.

The 28-PM model outperforms clinical parameters (TNM staging, macroscopic appearance, vascular tumor embolus) individually and combined, and adding clinical parameters improves performance by only ~1%.

The 28-PM risk score (cutoff 2.1) stratifies patients into high- and low-risk groups with different OS and DFS, and is an independent prognostic factor in multivariate Cox regression (HR 7.53, 95% CI 2.83-20.04, P=5.276e-5).

findings.evidence: The paper reports "95% confidence" intervals, but the code computes the interval with 5%/95% bounds (`confidence_lower = sorted_scores[int(0.05 * len(sorted_scores))]`) (and 1 similar line(s)), which is a 90% interval; no 2.5%/97.5% bounds appear anywhere in the code. Check whether the reported intervals are 90% intervals.
findings.question_for_authors: Are the reported confidence intervals 95% or 90% intervals?

findings.location: Results 'Comparison of the diagnostic performance...', p.3 vs data/GC-diagnosis-model/Biomarker_clinical.xlsx
findings.evidence: The paper reports single-marker sensitivities CA19-9 0.217, CA72-4 0.317, CEA 0.165 and any-abnormal 0.428. From Biomarker_clinical.xlsx Sheet1 (208 GC rows, all state=1) we get 0.1827 (34/186), 0.2404 (45/187), 0.149 (28/188) and 0.4279 (any of the three, 208 rows). The any-abnormal value reproduces exactly while the three single-marker values do not, so the single-marker denominators or the cut-offs used in the paper differ from the file; the paper does not state which subset was used.
findings.question_for_authors: Which patients and which cut-offs (CA19-9 27, CA72-4 6.9, CEA 5 U/mL) underlie the single-marker sensitivities 0.217 / 0.317 / 0.165?

findings.location: Methods 'Diagnostic prediction model' vs code/GC-diagnosis-model/run.ipynb cell 5
findings.evidence: Methods text states the LASSO penalty as 0.01; the released notebook instantiates ArgsClass(k=10, alpha=0.005). Our re-run shows the choice matters: with standardised features alpha=0.005 gives test-set AUROC 0.9693 and alpha=0.01 gives 0.9580 (bp_out/multiverse_results.csv).
findings.question_for_authors: Which LASSO alpha produced the reported 10-metabolite panel, 0.005 (code) or 0.01 (Methods)?

findings.location: Fig. 4b legend; Fig. 4d legend; code/GC-prognosis-model/run.ipynb cell 16
findings.evidence: The paper labels the prognostic intervals '95% CI' (Fig. 4b: 0.697-0.951; Fig. 4d c-index bars). The released bootstrap function computes the 5th and 95th percentiles (confidence_lower = sorted_scores[int(0.05*n)], confidence_upper = sorted_scores[int(0.95*n)]) and its own comment calls this a 90% interval; no 2.5/97.5 percentile appears in the code. The stored output prints 'Confidence interval for the score: [0.697 - 0.951]', i.e. the reported interval is the 90% interval.
findings.question_for_authors: Are the prognostic intervals in Fig. 4b and Fig. 4d 95% or 90% intervals?

findings.location: code/GC-prognosis-model/run.ipynb cell 9 (loop) and cell 10 (choice of 28 features)
findings.evidence: Cell 9 refits the random survival forest for i = 1..147 features and records rsf_sel.score(Xtest_sel, ytest) for every i; the paper's 28-metabolite panel is the i=28 point of that sweep, i.e. the feature count was read off test-set c-index. The released LASSO runs on raw relative abundances (values 1e-7 to 0.21) without scaling; at alpha=0.005 every coefficient is shrunk to zero (0 of 147 non-zero), so the released code cannot reproduce the 10-metabolite panel as written. Our re-run standardises the features inside each split (a documented substitute, bp_work/adapter.py) and then reproduces the reported AUROC (0.9693 vs 0.967).
findings.question_for_authors: Was the LASSO fitted on scaled or unscaled relative abundances, and with which sklearn version?

findings.evidence: Stage-stratified AUROCs are reported for stage IA/IB in test set 1 and stage IA in test set 2, but the per-stage sample sizes are not given in the text; from the released prediction files the stage IA subset of test set 1 has 16 GC patients and the stage IA subset of test set 2 has 11, so the reported 0.957 and 0.909 rest on very few cases.
